name: Kali (Bèlèl)
overview: The Kali of Bèlèl, a Mboum-speaking people, live as a minority among the Fulani, Dourou, Hausa, Beti, Basaa, Toupouri and Bamiléké. Having come from Mayo-Rey (Lugéré Baka) via Mbang, they keep a family chiefdom and live from farming and trade. The dzwùŋ dance accompanies circumcisions, millet threshing and funerals, and the millet festival, held twice a year, drives away disease.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Minority group among many neighbours (Fulani, Dourou, Hausa, Beti, Basaa, Toupouri, Bamiléké); people understand the other languages rather than speak them.
Kali is also spoken in the North and East, and in Chad and the Central African Republic.
Heterogeneous group, with many outsiders; marriages mostly endogamous, with women more often marrying outside.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: Ancestral land that belongs to them, with no particular religious dimension.
Having come from the Mayo-Rey (Lugéré Baka) via Mbang, they still have property there and return there to hunt.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: Kingship: the chiefdom belongs to a single family.
The village chief convenes, supported by the president of the Mboum dynamic association; consensus is sought.
Exchanges take place mainly within each group (men, women, young people), freely but with respect.
The brother's son inherits the property and the chiefdom; the sister's son may inherit property.
Mature men, regularly renewed, dig the graves.
The traditional chiefs are allied within an association. Formerly, a woman had to be fully covered to pass among men.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; the wife joins her husband's family. People marry around the age of 18.
The suitor brings firewood, farms and offers gifts; if the girl burns his wood, she has chosen him from among his rivals.
The bride price, paid to the father and mother, is paid once the wife is settled.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: No ancestor worship; the dzwùŋ is a symbolic place about ten kilometres from the paternal home.
The child is a gift from God; death is rest.

Taboos: incest, questions of inheritance. The boy does not lift the lid of the pot when his mother cooks; in the past, he did not cook, and girls did not go to football, to school, or to the place of circumcision.
A child who strikes his father must bring wood and kola to an elder who will plead for him; insulting a superior earns three months of isolation.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Men and women: farming and trade.
The land belongs to the chiefdom; it is requested orally or in writing.
Ancestral crafts: winnowing tray for millet (kàrì), kpò for keeping game or fish, large calabash for collecting honey, clay pots.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Gari, boubou, wrappers.
Traditional medicine remains in use, for lack of means and for its effectiveness.
Beauty: intelligence, wisdom and wealth for men; understanding and good lineage for women.
Courtship: coming from a respected and well-off family, having received a good upbringing.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Rhythms: dzwùŋ, ŋgòŋ, sìjùŋ, làbè, laoùlé, on the balafon and the tam-tam.
The dzwùŋ accompanies circumcisions, millet threshing and funerals; the làbè, the initiation of young girls.
Festivals: zàgá bàm, for the return of the rain; millet festival, in March and November, to drive away disease.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: The Kali have a sociopolitical organisation close to that of the Bamiléké.

sections.title: The names
items: Names follow clans, families and circumstances; people do not change their name, but add one on converting to Islam.
Among peers and friends, people call each other by name or by a pseudonym.

lessons.title: Who are the Kali (Bèlèl)? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Kali (Bèlèl) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Kali (Bèlèl) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Kali (Bèlèl) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Kali (Bèlèl) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Kali (Bèlèl) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Kali (Bèlèl) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Minority group among many neighbours (Fulani, Dourou, Haoussa, Beti, Basaa, Toupouri, Bamiléké); people understand the other languages rather than speak them. • Kali is also spoken in the North and East, and in Chad and the Central African Republic. • Heterogeneous group, with many outsiders; marriages mostly endogamous, with women more often marrying outside. • Ancestral land that belongs to them, with no particular religious dimension. • Having come from Mayo-Rey (Lugéré Baka) through Mbang, they still have property there and return there to hunt.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Kali of Bèlèl, a Mboum-speaking people, live as a minority among the Fulani, Dourou, Hausa, Beti, Basaa, Toupouri and Bamiléké. Having come from Mayo-Rey (Lugéré Baka) via Mbang, they keep a family chiefdom and live from farming and trade. The dzwùŋ dance accompanies circumcisions, millet threshing and funerals, and the millet festival, held twice a year, drives away disease.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Kali (Bèlèl) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Power and social organisation among the Kali (Bèlèl)
lessons.anelcac: Socio-political organisation, rules for living together
lessons.competence: Describe how the Kali (Bèlèl) organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.
lessons.situation: An important decision must be made for the whole Kali (Bèlèl) village. Who decides, and how?
lessons.materiel: The community's cultural profile, paper and felt-tip pens for the organisation chart.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe how the Kali (Bèlèl) organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “An important decision has to be made for the whole Kali (Bèlèl) village. Who decides, and how?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who holds authority? — How are decisions made (consensus, vote, the chief's decision)? — What rules of respect and deference are observed? — Which groups or societies play a particular role?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following points: • Kingship: the chiefdom belongs to a single family. • The village chief convenes, supported by the president of the Mboum dynamic association; consensus is sought. • Exchanges take place mostly within each group (men, women, young people), freely but with respect. • The brother's son inherits the property and the chiefdom; the sister's son may inherit some property. • Mature men, regularly replaced, dig the graves.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Kingship: the chiefdom belongs to a single family. The village chief convenes, supported by the president of the Mboum dynamic association; consensus is sought. Discussions take place mainly within each group (men, women, young people), freely but with respect.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-II — Cultural practices: ways of life
lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Kali (Bèlèl)
objectives: Linking food to the living environment
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Kali (Bèlèl), describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Kali (Bèlèl).
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Kali (Bèlèl), describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Kali (Bèlèl).” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: groundnut dish (déré), ɠòlè, gɛ̀tɛ̀rɛ̀. • Drinks: gbwá (bil-bil), pata (millet beer). • Men and women: farming and trade. • Ancestral crafts: winnowing tray for millet (kàrì), kpò for keeping game or fish, large calabash for harvesting honey, canaris.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Kali (Bèlèl) eat mainly déré, ɠòlè, gɛ̀tɛ̀rɛ̀. Traditional drinks: gbwá, millet beer. These foods are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Kali (Bèlèl): write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Birth, name and the passage to adulthood among the Kali (Bèlèl)
objectives: Explain the meaning of a birth

vocabulary.frenchText: “the one from whom the land is claimed”

lessons.competence: Explain how the Kali (Bèlèl) welcome a child, give the child a name and mark the child's entry into adulthood.
lessons.situation: A child has just been born in a Kali (Bèlèl) family. How will he be named, and how will he become an adult?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain how the Kali (Bèlèl) welcome a child, give it a name and mark its entry into adulthood.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A child has just been born in a Kali (Bèlèl) family. How will they be named, and how will they become an adult?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What does a birth mean for the community? — Who gives the name, when and how? — Can the name change during a lifetime? — When and how does one become a man or a woman?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Names follow clans, families and circumstances; one does not change name, but adds one on converting to Islam. • Among peers and friends, people call each other by name or by a nickname. • The child is a gift from God; death is rest. • Patrilineal kinship; the wife joins her husband's family. People marry around 18.

student.memo: Among the Kali (Bèlèl), traditional dances (dzwùŋ, làbè) accompany the great moments of life: celebrations, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: balafon, tam-tam. Festival(s): zàgá bàm, millet festival.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Kali (Bèlèl)
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Kali (Bèlèl), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Kali (Bèlèl). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Kali (Bèlèl), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Kali (Bèlèl). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • Men and women: farming and trade. • Land belongs to the chiefdom; it is requested orally or in writing. • Ancestral crafts: winnowing tray for millet (kàrì), kpò for keeping game or fish, large calabash for harvesting honey, canaris.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Men and women: farming and trade. Land belongs to the chiefdom; it is requested orally or in writing.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a two-column table (men / women) of the Kali (Bèlèl)'s activities, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Kali (Bèlèl)
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death

vocabulary.langText: soulever la marmite de sa mère

lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Kali (Bèlèl), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Kali (Bèlèl). Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Kali (Bèlèl), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Kali (Bèlèl). Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following points: • No ancestor worship; the dzwùŋ is a symbolic place about ten kilometres from the paternal home. • The child is a gift from God; death is rest. • Taboos: incest, inheritance matters. The boy does not lift the pot lid when his mother is cooking; in the past, he did not cook, and girls did not go to football, to school, or to the circumcision site. • A child who hits his father must bring firewood and kola nut to an elder who will plead for him; insulting a superior earns three months of isolation.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: No ancestor worship; the dzwùŋ is a symbolic place about ten kilometres from the paternal home. The child is a gift from God; death is rest.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Kali (Bèlèl) (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Discover what the Kali (Bèlèl) believe, the places they respect and the taboos they observe.

activities.title: I compare

student.memo: No ancestor worship; the dzwùŋ is a symbolic place about ten kilometres from the paternal home. The child is a gift from God; death is rest.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Kali
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Kali (Bèlèl) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Kali (Bèlèl) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Kali (Bèlèl) greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Kali (Bèlèl) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • The community's language is Kali. • Greeting formulae: Kwa᷅hi᷇ = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); Na᷅wa᷅be᷇le᷅le᷅ = morning greeting (one person); I᷅na᷅wa᷅be᷇le᷅le᷅ = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Bɸ᷅ u᷇, Se᷅le᷅, Sa᷇j, Ne᷄ɳ, di᷅bi᷄. • Among peers and friends, people call each other by name or by a pseudonym. • The Kali have a sociopolitical organisation close to that of the Bamiléké.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Kali are the first steps towards communicating with the Kali (Bèlèl). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Learn to greet, introduce yourself and count in Kali.

activities.title: I greet
activities.instruction: Learn the greeting formulas for morning, midday and evening.

activities.title: I introduce myself
activities.instruction: Say your name, where you are from and where you live.

activities.title: I count
activities.instruction: Count objects from 1 to 10.

activities.title: I pass on
activities.instruction: Teach a formula to a classmate or a family member.

student.memo: Greeting and counting in Kali are the first steps towards communicating with the Kali (Bèlèl). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.
